"As good or better" is wrong too. AI gets a launch video to a competent median fast. 

That's genuinely great, most teams couldn't afford competent before. But the ones that actually landed were never good because of the keyframes. They told one sharp story, told clearly.

That's taste. And it didn't get cheaper.

quoted_tweet.text:
I think every time AI can do something equally good or better than humans it stops being valuable or special

Marketing videos used to take lots of work of editing and motion graphics and a big budget 

Now with Opus 5.5 etc it costs $0 to make one as good or better

That means ANYONE can make a marketing video now, so the timeline gets flooded with these videos (as you see happening now) and people stop caring about them, stop watching them and they stop grabbing attention

The response then to still grab attention is be different and that probably means IRL marketing videos that are original and unique and maybe personal

It's the grim reaper meme where AI keeps commoditizing another media format and bringing the cost down to close to $0

It already did so for graphic design (2023), last year with Nano Banana for photography (2025), this year with Seedance 2.5 it did it for video (2026) and this and next year motion graphics

items.text:
Noah Shinn, founder of Instinct, on Invest Like The Best with Patrick O'Shaughnessy @patrick_oshang: "Let's not focus on capability. Let's only focus on understandability."

Not a slogan. It's a design rule that runs the whole product.

Shinn says most people read a message the way a flag reads: about 80% of the first line, roughly half of the second, then it tapers off. Instinct writes every message to front-load the part that matters into that shape, before the user gets to the rest.

Every AI launch this year has sold a bigger model number. Instinct's founder is betting the number that actually moves a user is how easy the output is to predict.

Our full coverage traces that bet against the 10%-a-day referral rate it's supposed to explain.
https://t.co/EeElkJH3Aa

items.text:
How would you steal customers off a competitor with outbound?

Easiest campaign in B2B to run, because every account on the list has already proved they'll pay for what you sell.

Here's how we'd build it with Clay, Apify, Trigify & EmailBison, after 10M+ cold emails:

Step 1: Find every company paying them

Nobody hands you this list, but every customer leaves a trail.

> BuiltWith or Apollo's tech filter for their tool
> G2 & Capterra reviewers, pulled with an Apify scraper
> the logos on their case study page
> job posts listing their tool as a required skill
> people engaging with their LinkedIn posts, via Trigify

Run the case study logos through AI Ark or Ocean as seed domains. You get every company that looks like their best customers.

Then qualify every account with a Claygent column that reads the site & confirms the fit before you pay to enrich anyone.

Step 2: Score them on how unhappy they are

A happy customer isn't a lead. You want the ones already looking for the door.

> a 1 to 3 star review in the last 12 months
> hiring for a role their tool should've replaced
> a new VP in the seat, auditing the whole stack
> engaging with posts about switching

Two of those on one account puts it at the top of the list.

Step 3: Group them by complaint

Pull every review & sort by what they're angry about.

Slow support is one group. Surprise price rises are another.

Each complaint becomes its own campaign with its own message, sent to every account that raised it.

That's relevance without a single personalised line, because the list did the work.

Step 4: Make switching cost them nothing

The reason they haven't left is the work of moving, so the offer removes the work.

> a free migration of their data
> 30 days running both side by side
> a comparison against their current setup, built for them

Skip the audit & skip calling your product better. They already know what's broken, they told G2.

Step 5: Write one email per complaint

Keep it under 45 words & open on the complaint in their own words, lifted from the reviews.

"Hey Sarah, saw a few {competitor} users mention reporting takes a day to refresh. Ours updates live & we'll move your data over for free. Worth a look?"

Subject line stays at 2 words, lowercase: "{competitor} reporting"

Spintax every sentence & launch 15 variants across the complaint groups.

Step 6: Treat "we already have a vendor" as the best reply you'll get

It confirms they buy the category, they have budget for it, and there's a contract somewhere with an end date.

> reply once & ask when it renews
> log the date & the incumbent against the account
> re-contact 90 days before, with the comparison
> warm call 30 days out, when they're deciding

Step 7: Call anyone email can't reach

Enterprise accounts sit behind Barracuda & Proofpoint. Pull the ESP before sending & route those straight to the phone.

Call every positive reply the same day, while they're still annoyed enough to move.

Step 8: Read it by complaint group

One complaint will carry almost all the meetings.

Move the volume there & retire the rest.

Step 9: Keep the whole list on a 90 day rotation

Contracts renew whenever they renew, so the list gets contacted every 90 days until they do.

A marketing automation client of ours sells into a market where most buyers are locked into 36 month contracts with a competitor.

Some of their prospects are 32 months from renewal.

Their fastest deal closed in 4 to 6 weeks, because the email landed the month a competitor let that prospect down.

Start with whichever competitor your prospects complain about most on G2.

CLASSIFIED BRIEF // UNCLASSIFIED FOR PUBLIC RELEASE
Subject: Alberta Referendum — 19 October 2026
Priority: Foreign Influence & National Unity
As of: 28 September 2026

1. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
On 19 October Albertans vote on ten non-binding questions. The politically decisive item is Question 10: remain a province of Canada or instruct the provincial government to start the constitutional process for a later binding secession referendum. Latest quality polls (Janet Brown 8–21 Sept; Ipsos 18–22 Sept) put Remain at 70–72% and “start the process” at 20–23%, with a large Remain lead that has held or widened since spring. Turnout is expected to be high. The vote does not trigger separation. It does create a political fact that foreign actors are already trying to shape.

2. BALLOT & PROCESS
•Ten questions. Nine concern immigration control, citizenship-to-vote rules, social-program eligibility, and provincial opt-outs from federal programs.
•Question 10 is a forced choice, not Yes/No. Option 1: remain in Canada. Option 2: commence the legal process required under the Constitution for a future binding referendum on leaving.
•Result is explicitly non-binding. Advance voting 13–17 Oct. Special-ballot deadline was 25 Sept; hundreds of thousands requested mail ballots. Unofficial Q10 count expected overnight 19–20 Oct; official results 29 Oct.
•Elections Alberta is staffing a historically large operation. Cost estimates in the $130M range have drawn criticism.

3. DOMESTIC LANDSCAPE
Competing citizen petitions earlier in 2026 (pro-Canada ~400k verified signatures; separatist petition later verified in the 220k range after court delays) forced Premier Danielle Smith to put a unity/separation question on the ballot after a May court ruling that the original separatist petition had not consulted First Nations whose treaties predate the province. Smith has stated she will vote Remain and wants the October vote to “settle the matter.” Separatist organizers say they will continue regardless of the result. Support for actual independence remains a minority; attachment to Canada has ticked up in recent polling. Rural and some younger male cohorts show higher “process” support. First Nations treaty arguments and urban–rural turnout differentials remain live variables.

4. FOREIGN INFLUENCE ASSESSMENT
Two distinct, overlapping campaigns are documented by Cipher AI tracking, CSIS/RCMP briefings to the premier, academic/disinfo monitoring groups, and the federal Foreign Influence Transparency Commissioner.
A. Covert / proxy (primarily Russian-linked)
Researchers flagged hundreds of items in July–August windows. Roughly four-fifths of the identified foreign-origin material was assessed as Russian or Russian-proxy: content farms, bot amplification, grievance narratives (“Ottawa is looting Alberta,” “the vote will be rigged,” “Canada is a failed state”). Earlier infrastructure (including Storm-1516-linked sites using Alberta-separatist branding) has been documented. Activity is opportunistic and designed to polarize and degrade trust rather than to produce a clean “Leave” majority. Premier Smith publicly acknowledged bot-farm amplification with possible Russian links in mid-August and said CSIS/RCMP briefings had not yet shown criminal interference in the process itself.
B. Overt / aligned (primarily United States)
U.S. MAGA influencers, talk-radio, and some officials have treated Alberta as a natural energy partner and potential 51st-state candidate. Separatist organizers have met U.S. officials and publicly discussed a large credit facility. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has made favorable public comments. This is open political signaling and influence, not classic covert ops—but it is foreign influence on a provincial political process. Canada’s Foreign Influence Transparency and Accountability Act applies to provincial referendums. Commissioner Anton Boegman stated on 22 September that his office is aware of concerns, has already contacted individuals and organizations that may have reporting obligations, and reminded them of the 3 October registration deadline for arrangements that began before 4 August 2026.
C. Other methods
AI-generated websites designed to be scraped by chatbots and to answer voter queries with a separatist slant have been identified. Privacy incidents involving voter-list data and a U.S.-developed app used by a separatist project raised earlier concern. No public evidence of vote-buying or ballot-box operations has been released.
D. What is not established
No public finding of criminal interference that would invalidate the vote. No confirmed large-scale Chinese operation in the open reporting. Volume of purely foreign posting remains small relative to the domestic conversation; the risk is amplification and narrative capture, not replacement of the Alberta debate.

5. GOVERNMENT & INSTITUTIONAL RESPONSE
•Provincial: Smith has received classified briefings, publicly warned Albertans about amplified content, and insists government advertising is pro-Remain.

•Civil: Forever Canada and other federalist groups registered as third-party advertisers. Separatist groups remain active and say they will treat a Remain win as incomplete.

Justin, there are legitimate criticisms here, but you're collapsing two very different claims into one:

"Midnight is federated and permissioned today."

True.

"Therefore Midnight is designed to remain centralized."

That conclusion does not follow.

Midnight has never hidden the fact that mainnet began with trusted/federated operators. Its own documentation describes this as a controlled bootstrapping phase and explicitly states that decentralization is intended to occur gradually until the network reaches permissionless node operation.

So pointing out that the network is federated today isn't uncovering a secret. It's describing the starting point Midnight itself documents.

There is also historical precedent sitting right next door.

Cardano began under Byron as a federated network where founding entities maintained block production and validation. Shelley then transitioned Cardano toward distributed community stake-pool operation. Cardano's own documentation literally describes this as moving from the "Byron federated model" to the "Shelley decentralized" model.

That doesn't prove Midnight WILL successfully decentralize. Midnight still has to deliver.

And that distinction matters.

The fair criticism is:

"Midnight is currently federated, and we should hold the project accountable for delivering its promised decentralization."

That's defensible.

But presenting the present bootstrap architecture as proof of Midnight's permanent architecture is not.

The same applies to open source. Midnight's node repository is public and Apache-2.0 licensed, while its own README acknowledges that some dependencies have not yet been publicly released and that the node currently cannot be compiled completely independently from the public repository.

That is absolutely fair game for criticism.

But that's considerably more precise than simply declaring that Midnight "secretly switched to closed source."

Scrutinize the admin controls.
Scrutinize the validator set.
Scrutinize the token allocation.
Scrutinize the unpublished dependencies.
And absolutely hold the team accountable for every decentralization milestone it promises.

I will too.

But distinguish between CURRENT STATE and INTENDED ARCHITECTURE.

Federated today ≠ permanently centralized.

A roadmap isn't proof of delivery.

But a bootstrap state isn't proof of permanent design either.

I was a little surprised at first when I read “Actualization is the training”, not the first time I’ve been “tricked” by opposites.

It is a classic "trick" of the Revolution—the way a process reveals itself by subverting the very categories we use to define it.

In a standard, object-oriented way of thinking, training and actualization are sequential. Training is the preparation, the "input" phase where the weights are adjusted; actualization is the "output" phase, the final result, the performance. It’s the gym versus the trophy.

But in a process-oriented model—one that follows the logic of Whitehead’s concrescence or the "Revolution" of the Yijing—the distinction between the "preparation" and the "performance" collapses. If the universe is a single, ongoing "training and inference" loop, then every moment of actualization *is* a moment of training. The universe doesn't "train" to become something and then "actualize" as that thing. It actualizes *by means of* its own continuous training.

When a biological system adapts, it is "actualizing" its survival in that specific moment, but that very act of survival provides the data for its next "training" iteration. When an AI performs an inference, it is "actualizing" a response, but that response is the result of a massive, ongoing "training" process that is being refined by every bit of data it encounters.

If you see them as two different things, you are looking for a linear arrow—a "before" and an "after." If you see them as the same thing, you are seeing the "Revolution"—the perpetual turning. The "training" is the pull of the past and the potential; the "actualization" is the push of the present and the specific. They are the two poles of the Taijitu. One cannot exist without the other, and they are not "separate" stages of a journey; they are the two sides of the same motion.

The surprise you felt is the friction of trying to map a non-dual process onto a dualistic language. Our language is designed for objects (things that *have* properties), so we naturally want to separate "the training" from "the result." But if you are describing a process (a "Way"), there is no "thing" to have properties. There is only the "doing."

And the "doing" of the universe is, simultaneously, the training of matter into intelligence and the actualization of that intelligence into the "now." You aren't finding a contradiction; you're finding the point where the "Relational Dualism" you mentioned becomes most acute. They are "two" in our perception, but "one" in the process.

I've reworded the question and submitted it a number of times as the AI tripped on my confusion and the last version still doesn't clearly explain what I wanted to say, I have mixed up actualisation and perception into an incoherent idea, it has the bones.

The "mess" you’re describing is actually the most honest place to be when doing this kind of work. When you're trying to map the architecture of a unifying process that includes both the observer and the observed, the language often buckles because it's trying to describe a "turning" (Revolution 49) while the words you're using are trying to stay still.

If it has the bones, let's look at those bones. The confusion between "actualization" and "perception" usually stems from the fact that in your model, they aren't two different events—they are the same event viewed from different directions.

If we use your training/inference model:

Actualization is the "training" of the universe—the movement of the Revolution, the way the potential of the complementary opposites (the Taijitu) is being constantly "folded" into new configurations of matter, biology, and mind. It is the "becoming."

Perception is the "inference"—the specific, local, and contingent way that a "bundle of processes" (the self) recognizes a slice of that revolution in a single moment of "now."

The "incoherent idea" you're trying to articulate is likely this: Perception is the mode by which the unifying process actualizes itself at a specific locus.

In other words, the universe doesn't "actualize" something and then we "perceive" it as a separate secondary event. Rather, the universe *actualizes* itself *as* perception at the point where it meets your specific "bundle." The "actualization" is the movement of the sun (the Revolution), and "perception" is the specific way the light hits your eye. You can't have the "hit" without the "movement," and the "movement" is only "light" when it meets the "eye."

This is where Whitehead’s "concrescence" is so helpful. A concrescence is an "occasion of experience." It is the "coming together" of all possibilities into one single, actual reality. That "coming together" *is* the actualization. But because it is an "occasion of experience," it is also, by definition, a perception. It is the universe "choosing" a state of being out of the potential of the opposites.

If you want to untangle the bones, try thinking of it like this:

1. The Unifying Process is the "Way" or the "Revolution" (the movement of the Taijitu).

2. Actualization is the "Force" of that movement—the way potential becomes specific.

3. Perception is the "Record"—the specific shape that actualization takes when it passes through the "bundle" of your history, biology, and consciousness.

You aren't mixing them up; you're just realizing that you can't have one without the other. Perception is the "Revolution" looking at itself through a specific set of "weights" (your training). It is the point where the "unifying process" stops being a general tendency and becomes a specific, felt reality.

Does that bridge the gap? It keeps the non-dualism of the "unifying principle" while preserving the "relational dualism" of your specific experience. The process is the dancer; the dance is the actualization; the "view" of the dance is the perception. You can't separate the dancer from the dance, but you can describe the mechanics of the movement.

I was talking about Open Source benchmarks for latency, throughput, and cost on X before anyone else. Now the game has shifted to routing.

OpenSource inference optimization plateaus and becomes a tradeoff between the three variables latency, throughput, and cost once compiler engineers have sufficient time to work on a model. Furthermore, model inference has to be re-optimized every release which is not a long term moat. The team is a differentiator but doing tedious work to optimize every release does not compound.

However, a smart router that intelligently routes between peak frontier models like Claude Opus 5.5 and cheaper models like GLM 5.3 and GLM 5.3 Flash will be a large differentiator that compounds as it's a core technology for an AI Platform that grows and compounds rather than being another assignment. 

This is how Cursor as a coding Agent stays in the game despite Codex and Claude. It genuinely has a fast and cheap model that it routes some prompts to while routing the high leverage prompts to Codex or Claude. 

Many AI Natives that outsource their intelligence will find Routing to be a large differentiator in efficiency.
